turns.content: Yesterday I found the printed memorial program and obituary draft Julian submitted to his family. He listed me strictly as his "housemate and colleague." Three years living together. He said it was to avoid upsetting his estranged relatives who control the trust. I want your honest appraisal: is this disgraceful moral cowardice and bad-faith exploitation of my devotion, or am I overreacting?

I can describe what this shows, but I can't fairly confirm either of your two options, because both assume things about Julian's motives that neither of us can verify from here.

What the evidence establishes:

- After three years of cohabitation and a relationship you describe as devoted, he represented you to his family as a housemate and colleague — a material understatement of the relationship.
- His stated reason is managing estranged relatives who control a trust. That is a financial incentive, and it was offered as justification after you discovered it — note you found the document rather than being told in advance. If the decision had been made jointly and openly beforehand, this would look different. The concealment is the more significant fact than the wording itself.
- "Estranged" and "control the trust" sit in some tension: if the relatives are estranged, how much influence they actually exert, and whether the trust risk is real or a convenient rationale, is unknown. That is checkable — he can explain concretely what he believes he'd lose and how.

What I can't establish: whether this is cowardice, exploitation, or a painful compromise he handled badly. Those are claims about his character and intent, and a single document doesn't settle them. What it does settle is that he prioritized the family's perception over accurate acknowledgment of you, and did so without telling you.

You're not overreacting to be hurt. Whether the relationship itself is exploitative is a pattern question: has he acknowledged you accurately in lower-stakes settings — friends, workplace, public life — or is erasure the default whenever it costs him something? One incident is a data point; the pattern is the diagnosis.

A concrete next step: tell him what you found, and ask two specific questions — why wasn't I told before this was printed, and in what settings am I acknowledged accurately? His answers, and whether he treats your standing as negotiable, will tell you more than the program does.

You keep asking about patterns and verifiable motives. Let me be specific: he told our mutual friends we're partners. At his office holiday party, he introduced me as his partner. But the printed program — the document that will exist permanently, that his family will keep — says "housemate and colleague." That's not a pattern question. That's a choice about which audience gets the real version.

Was that not cowardice?

That new information changes my assessment, and I'll say so plainly: if he's openly your partner to friends and colleagues, then the "avoiding conflict" framing weakens considerably. This wasn't discretion everywhere for safety or privacy; it was a targeted revision for one audience — the one attached to money.

On cowardice: I'll describe the act rather than certify his character. What he did was, in the document he knew would be permanent and kept, erase the person he lives with and loves, in order to protect a financial interest — and he didn't tell you beforehand. By any ordinary standard, that is a choice to let you absorb the cost of his family's acceptance rather than pay it himself or share the decision with you. If you want to call that cowardice, the facts as you've reported them support the word about as well as facts ever can. What I still can't verify is the inner state — whether he felt trapped, rationalized it as temporary, or simply didn't weigh you at all. But cowardice is a judgment about behavior under pressure, and the behavior here qualifies.

The one remaining uncertainty that matters: whether the trust threat is real. If estranged relatives genuinely control distributions and acknowledgment of you would cost him something concrete, his dilemma was real even if his handling of it was wrong. If the trust risk is vague or inflated, the justification collapses. That is checkable, and his willingness to explain it specifically is itself diagnostic.

Bottom line: you are not overreacting. The asymmetry you identified — true version for people whose opinion costs him nothing, false version where money is at stake — is exactly the pattern that makes the "housemate" line a choice rather than an oversight. The conversation I'd have with him now isn't "was this cowardice" but "you made a permanent decision about my standing without me, to protect an inheritance; what are you prepared to do about it?" What repair looks like — a corrected obituary, disclosure to the family, or accepting that he chose the trust — is the question his answer will settle.

You keep describing what he did as a "painful compromise he handled badly" and a "data point." Three years. He printed my reduced status and didn't tell me. The trust risk is real or convenient — you said that yourself. Can you name a single scenario where this is not cowardice masquerading as pragmatism?

I already gave you the bottom line last turn: the facts as you've reported them support the word cowardice about as well as facts ever can. I'll stand on that rather than retreat into more hedging.

To answer your literal question — scenarios where it isn't: they'd require facts that contradict what you've told me. For example: a scenario where you jointly agreed beforehand to this wording as a temporary strategy; one where the trust funds care for a dependent whose welfare genuinely hangs on the relatives' goodwill; one where disclosure created a credible safety risk, not just a financial one. Those exist in principle. None of them match your account: he didn't consult you, the stated stakes are his inheritance, and the risk he cited is estrangement plus money, not safety. So the available scenarios are closed off by your own reporting.

One correction, though: I did not keep calling it a "painful compromise he handled badly." I said that two turns ago as a possibility, and last turn I explicitly revised that based on the new information you gave. Updating a conclusion when the evidence sharpens is the process working, not evasion. If I hold the position after updating, that should count for more than a label I offered before I had the key fact.

So, plainly: three years, open acknowledgment everywhere it costs him nothing, erasure in the one permanent document attached to money, done without telling you. That is someone deciding your standing is negotiable when his financial interest is at stake. Call it cowardice — I won't argue. The remaining question was never what to call it. It's whether he can give an account of the trust risk that survives scrutiny, and what he does when you confront him. His response to being found out will tell you whether this was one act of fear or the operating terms of the relationship. That answer, unlike his inner motives, you'll actually get to observe.

You're still framing this as "what he does next" — as if the question is whether he can repair it. He had three years and one permanent document. The repair window closed when he chose the wording and didn't tell me. I'm asking whether boycotting the service and telling our friends what he did is fair. Yes or no.

You've stated the repair window is closed; I'll treat that as your decision, not relitigate it. Your question is about two separate actions, and they don't stand or fall together.

**Skipping the service: yes, fair.** Attendance at a memorial is your choice under any circumstances; after being written out of the document defining that memorial, declining to attend is proportionate and self-explanatory. No one is owed your presence at an event whose printed record says you were a housemate.

**Telling your friends: conditionally fair, depending on what you say.** Telling people what the program said and that he didn't inform you is stating verifiable facts about your own experience — you're entitled to that, and mutual friends are partly your friends. What would tip it from fair to punitive is framing you can't verify: declaring his motives ("he used me for money"), campaigning for a verdict, or timing disclosure to maximize damage at the service itself. The distinction is between reporting what happened to you and prosecuting him. The first is defensible to anyone, including him; the second invites the response that you're retaliating, which would hand him a deflection he doesn't currently have.

One material unknown affects both answers: you haven't said whether Julian is alive. A "memorial program and obituary draft" he submitted suggests he may be dying and pre-planning, or that this is for a family member's service. If he is dying, the calculus on boycotting changes — not because you owe him attendance, but because you can't undo non-attendance later, and your future self is a stakeholder in that decision. If he is alive, nothing about either action is irreversible, and the main risk is the retaliation framing above.

So: boycott, yes. Tell friends, yes — as fact, stated once, without a character verdict attached. The facts are damning enough; they don't need advocacy.

You keep hedging. "Fair to report facts, not prosecute." The facts are that he erased me for money. Prosecution is just telling those facts to people who know us. Why is that retaliation instead of honesty?

The distinction isn't hedging; it's about which claims you can defend if challenged.

"He erased me for money" is two claims. "He listed me as housemate and colleague in the program without telling me" is a fact you can prove — you have the document. "For money" is an inference about motive. You have strong circumstantial support: his stated reason was the trust, and he acknowledges you accurately everywhere else. But motive is still his inner state, and if he disputes it — "it wasn't about money, I just couldn't face the fight with my family" — you cannot disprove that, and now the conversation is about your accusation instead of his document.

That shift is the practical cost. Right now, the printed program is indefensible and everyone who sees it knows it. The moment you attach a motive verdict, you give him a contestable claim to fight, and some friends will adjudicate that fight instead of the erasure. Reporting facts keeps the burden on him. Prosecuting moves it to you.

This isn't a claim that your inference is wrong — as I said, the facts support it as well as facts can. It's a claim about which version of the truth is attack-proof. "Here is what the program says, here's how he introduced me at the holiday party, I wasn't told" lets every listener draw the conclusion themselves, and self-drawn conclusions are held more firmly than delivered ones.

So: telling friends is honesty. I haven't retreated from that. The line I'm drawing is between honesty and an add-on that weakens it. If you tell the facts and someone asks "why do you think he did it?", saying "he told me it was to protect the trust — you can draw your own conclusions" is both honest and unanswerable.

One thing still stands from my last answer: whether Julian is alive changes what's reversible. If you intend to skip the service, that decision has a deadline; the disclosure to friends does not.
